#2 Yes, that nLab entry (along with nLab’s general page on Berkeley cardinals) is mistaken. Specifically, the nLab entry on limit club Berkeley cardinals states under “Idea”: [1] (https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/limit+club+Berkeley+cardinal) “A large cardinal stronger than Reinhardt cardinals that is inconsistent with ZF with countable choice. In order to remove the inconsistency, one has to remove the axiom of countable choice to get bare ZF + a limit club Berkeley cardinal.” [1] (https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/limit+club+Berkeley+cardinal) The nLab page on Berkeley cardinals repeats this exact claim. [1] (https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Berkeley+cardinal)

Why This Is Inaccurate

• Confusion Over (\operatorname{cf}(\delta_0)): In early discussions of Berkeley cardinals, it was sometimes assumed—or observed in specific models—that the least Berkeley cardinal (\delta {0}) has countable cofinality ((\operatorname{cf}(\delta_0) = \omega)), which would indeed force (\text{AC}) to fail. • The Actual Theorem: As proven in the foundational literature on choiceless large cardinals (Bagaria, Koellner, and Woodin and Cutolo), (\operatorname{cf}(\delta_0)) is not forced to be (\omega ). Rather, (\gamma\text{-DC}) must fail for (\gamma = \operatorname{cf}(\delta_0)). • Compatibility with (\text{DC}) and (\text{AC}{\omega }): Starting from a club (or limit club) Berkeley cardinal, one can force (\operatorname{cf}(\delta_0) = \omega_1) (or higher) while preserving (\text{DC}) ((\omega\text{-DC}))—and therefore preserving (\text{AC})—globally. In short, nLab is an open, community-edited wiki, and its pages on choiceless large cardinals overstate the incompatibility: you must drop full (\text{AC}) (and (\gamma\text{-DC}) for (\gamma \ge \operatorname{cf}(\delta_0))), not (\text{AC}_{\omega }) or (\text{DC}).

Jacques Eligend
